steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: GCSE Latin prose set texts are prescribed by each exam board and change every two years. You must check which texts are current for your year of examination.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Common prose authors include Caesar (De Bello Gallico), Cicero (speeches and letters), Tacitus (Annales), Pliny the Younger (Letters), and Livy (Ab Urbe Condita).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Caesar's De Bello Gallico describes his conquest of Gaul (58-50 BC): key themes include Roman imperialism, leadership, and the clash between Roman and barbarian cultures.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cicero's works include political speeches (In Catilinam against Catiline) and personal letters that reveal late Republican politics and daily life.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: Name three common prose authors studied at GCSE Latin. | Q: What is the subject of Caesar's De Bello Gallico? | Q: What was the Catilinarian conspiracy and which author wrote about it?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Caesar (De Bello Gallico), Cicero (speeches and letters), Tacitus (Annales), Pliny the Younger (Letters), Livy (Ab Urbe Condita) (any three). | Caesar's own account of his military campaigns in Gaul (58-50 BC), covering battles, negotiations with Gallic tribes, and expeditions to Britain and Germany. | A plot led by Catiline to overthrow the Roman Republic in 63 BC, exposed by Cicero in his In Catilinam speeches. Cicero's four orations against Catiline are a key set text option.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always check which set texts are prescribed for YOUR exam year — studying the wrong text loses all marks on that question. Learn the historical context thoroughly: who wrote it, when, why, and for what audience — this is essential for the 10-mark context questions. For each set text, prepare notes on: key events, character portrayal, author's purpose, literary techniques, and themes. Practise translating the prescribed passages until you can do so fluently — translation questions test both language and literature knowledge.
